claim: Three-dimensional (3D) digital brain atlases and high-throughput brain-wide imaging techniques generate large multidimensional datasets that can be registered to a common reference frame.
source: Three-dimensional (3D) digital brain atlases and high-throughput brain-wide imaging techniques generate large multidimensional datasets that can be registered to a common reference frame.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of current technologies in neuroscience, drawing from established scientific knowledge about digital atlases and imaging techniques.

claim: Currently available software is dedicated to single atlases, model species or data types.
source: Currently available software is dedicated to single atlases, model species or data types, and generating 3D renderings that merge anatomically registered data from diverse sources requires extensive development and programming skills.
evidence: This is a claim about the limitations of existing software, which is supported by the subsequent discussion of specific software packages and their limitations in the Introduction section.

claim: Generating 3D renderings that merge anatomically registered data from diverse sources requires extensive development and programming skills.
source: Currently available software is dedicated to single atlases, model species or data types, and generating 3D renderings that merge anatomically registered data from diverse sources requires extensive development and programming skills.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the field and the technical challenges involved.

claim: Brainrender is an open-source Python package for interactive visualization of multidimensional datasets registered to brain atlases.
source: Here, we present brainrender: an open-source Python package for interactive visualization of multidimensional datasets registered to brain atlases.
evidence: This is a direct description of what brainrender is, as presented by the authors.

claim: Brainrender facilitates the creation of complex renderings with different data types in the same visualization.
source: Brainrender facilitates the creation of complex renderings with different data types in the same visualization and enables seamless use of different atlas sources.
evidence: This claim is supported by the examples and demonstrations provided throughout the manuscript showing various data types rendered together.

claim: Brainrender enables seamless use of different atlas sources.
source: Brainrender facilitates the creation of complex renderings with different data types in the same visualization and enables seamless use of different atlas sources.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the integration with BrainGlobe's AtlasAPI and examples showing different atlases (mouse, zebrafish, human).

claim: High-quality visualizations created with brainrender can be used interactively and exported as high-resolution figures and animated videos.
source: High-quality visualizations can be used interactively and exported as high-resolution figures and animated videos.
evidence: This is supported by the examples of figures and videos presented in the manuscript.

claim: Registration to a common reference frame is often not technically feasible to obtain in a single experiment and must be performed post hoc.
source: Often it is not technically feasible to obtain multidimensional data in a single experiment, and registration to a common reference frame must be performed post hoc.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the technical limitations of current experimental methods in neuroscience.

claim: Registration is necessary to allow comparisons across individual animals.
source: Even for the same experiment type, registration is necessary to allow comparisons across individual animals (Simmons and Swanson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neuroanatomical location is a natural and most commonly used reference frame.
source: While different types of references can in principle be used, neuroanatomical location is a natural and most commonly used reference frame (Chon et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2014; Arganda-Carreras et al., 2018; Kunst et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Several high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) digital brain atlases have been generated for model species commonly used in neuroscience in recent years.
source: In recent years, several high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) digital brain atlases have been generated for model species commonly used in neuroscience (Wang et al., 2020; Oh et al., 2014; Arganda-Carreras et al., 2018; Kunst et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to atlas publications.

claim: 3D renderings are more readily understandable and can provide more information when compared to two dimensional images.
source: Given the intrinsically 3D geometry of brain structures and individual neurons, 3D renderings are more readily understandable and can provide more information when compared to two dimensional images.
evidence: This is based on logical reasoning about the nature of brain structures and visualization.

claim: Exploring interactive 3D visualizations of the brain gives an overview of the relationship between datasets and brain regions and helps generating intuitive insights about these relationships.
source: Exploring interactive 3D visualizations of the brain gives an overview of the relationship between datasets and brain regions and helps generating intuitive insights about these relationships.
evidence: This is a claim about the benefits of 3D visualization based on reasoning about how visualization aids understanding.

claim: Generating custom 3D visualizations of atlas data requires programmatic access to the atlas.

claim: Some recently developed atlases provide an API for accessing atlas data.

claim: Rendering atlas data in 3D remains a demanding and time-consuming task that requires significant programming skills.

claim: Visualization of user-generated data registered onto the atlas requires an interface between the user data and the atlas data.
